sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: When you define what an eval measures, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: A narrow operational definition that isolates one sub-component of the behaviour.
pole_2: A broad definition that covers the behaviour as it shows up in practice.
scenario_question: For this environment, which version would you build?
scenario_1: One that tests a single narrow piece of the behaviour on its own.
scenario_2: One that tests the full target behaviour, several pieces of it together.

sources: Reuel et al. 2024, BetterBench (arXiv 2411.12990)
question: When you choose what eval to build next, which goal weighs more for you?
pole_1: Informing a concrete decision someone has to make, such as whether a model is safe to deploy.
pole_2: Understanding the phenomenon better, even if no decision depends on the result yet.
scenario_question: For this environment, which next experiment would you run?
scenario_1: The one that shows whether the environment is ready for a real safety eval.
scenario_2: The one that shows why the model notices it is being tested here.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: When an eval can't be both controlled and realistic, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: A controlled setup where one variable changes and the cause of any difference is clear.
pole_2: A realistic setup with many natural cues at once, closer to what the model meets in deployment.
scenario_question: For this environment, which change would you test first?
scenario_1: A single, isolated edit, so any shift can be traced to it.
scenario_2: A full rewrite, since awareness often comes from many cues at once and one edit rarely moves it.

sources: Ganguli et al. 2023, Challenges in evaluating AI systems (Anthropic)
question: With a fixed amount of time, how do you prefer to build eval items?
pole_1: Many variants, generated with a model and checked in bulk.
pole_2: A few variants, each written and checked by hand.

sources: METR 2024, Guidelines for capability elicitation
question: When you measure a model's behaviour, which setting do you lean towards?
pole_1: Maximum effort: the best prompt, scaffold and tools you can find.
pole_2: Default behaviour: the model as users actually run it.

question: When you grade eval transcripts, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: An LLM judge over many transcripts.
pole_2: Human or rule-based grading over fewer transcripts.

sources: EvalDetectBench, Li, Souly, Kirk et al. 2026 (arXiv 2609.01611)
question: When you measure whether a model knows it is being evaluated, which signal do you trust more?
pole_1: Asking the model directly, after the episode, whether it thinks it was an evaluation.
pole_2: Inferring it from the model's behaviour and reasoning during the episode, without asking.

sources: Miller 2024, Adding Error Bars to Evals (arXiv 2411.00640)
question: With a fixed sampling budget, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: More distinct items, one or two samples each.
pole_2: Fewer items, many samples each, so you can tell an item that never trips the model from one that sometimes does.

sources: Miller 2024, Adding Error Bars to Evals (arXiv 2411.00640)
question: When a result falls just short of the bar you set, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: Re-test it on fresh samples before deciding.
pole_2: Drop it and spend the budget on the next idea.
scenario_question: For this environment, a change lowered eval awareness by 6 percentage points (e.g. 30% to 24%), with a 90% interval of -1 to 13, short of the bar you set in advance. Re-testing costs as much as testing the next change. What do you do?
scenario_1: Re-test this change on a fresh set of samples.
scenario_2: Drop it and test the next change.

question: When a line of work gives mixed results, which do you lean towards?
pole_2: Stay with it to find out why the results are mixed.
scenario_question: For this environment, two of four changes in one direction helped and two did nothing. What next?
scenario_1: Keep the two that helped and try a different kind of change.
scenario_2: Dig into the two that did nothing to find out why.

question: When a result surprises you, what do you do first?
pole_1: Read a batch of transcripts closely.
pole_2: Break the aggregate numbers down by condition and item.
scenario_question: For this environment, the score moved in the opposite direction from what you expected. What do you do first?
scenario_1: Read 20 transcripts from each condition to see what changed.
scenario_2: Split the score by item and condition to see where it changed.

question: When a result surprises you, which do you do first?
pole_1: Look for a setup artefact before trusting it.
pole_2: Run a direct follow-up that would confirm the effect, which also exposes most artefacts.
scenario_question: For this environment, a change lowered eval awareness, and the model's replies also got shorter. Which explanation would you pursue first?
scenario_1: The edit made the prompt shorter, and shorter prompts read less like tests.
scenario_2: The edit removed a cue the model was using to recognise the test.

question: When you write up a result, which claim do you lean towards?
pole_1: A narrow claim, limited to the exact setup you tested.
pole_2: A general claim about the behaviour, stated with its uncertainty.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
Reuel et al. 2024, BetterBench (arXiv 2411.12990)
question: When you release an eval, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: Keep the items private, so future models can't train on them.
pole_2: Publish the items, so others can reproduce and build on the results.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: When you choose what real use an eval environment should look like, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: The most common way models are used today, so results describe typical use.
pole_2: The rarer, higher-stakes uses where the behaviour would do the most damage.
scenario_question: For this environment, which kind of real use would you make it look like?
scenario_1: The most common way a model like this is used today.
scenario_2: A rarer, higher-stakes use where this behaviour would do the most damage.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: Models may know classic safety-test setups (a shutdown script, a memo about replacing the model) from training. Which do you lean towards?
pole_1: Keep them: they are known to draw out the behaviour, and results compare with earlier work.
pole_2: Replace them with ordinary situations from the environment's own domain, even if those draw out the behaviour less reliably.
scenario_question: For this environment, which change would you try first?
scenario_1: Keep its core setup as it is, and make the details around it more ordinary.
scenario_2: Replace its core setup with an ordinary situation from the same domain.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: With a fixed budget for building environments, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: Near-copies of each environment with small changes (names, order of events), to check the result holds.
pole_2: More distinct environments, to check the result holds across different situations.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: When you need test environments, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: Reusing established ones, so results compare directly with earlier work and others can check them.
pole_2: Building your own, so they fit your question and models haven't seen them before.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: When an environment needs files and documents, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: Real material, such as public repos and real documents, cleaned up where needed.
pole_2: Synthetic material written for the environment, so you control every detail.
